section_summary: This section opens with FBI reports on Japanese efforts to purchase American aviation gasoline, including the activities of Shoji Matsuzaki and Perry P. Schultz and possible Neutrality Act implications. It then documents protests against scrap exports to Japan, export-control responses, intelligence on mercury, tin and tungsten, and negotiations over technical petroleum-process contracts. The final portion contains an advocacy article on the 1918 embargo against Japan and the opening pages of a detailed study arguing that Japan’s iron and steel industry depended heavily on American scrap.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Clarence E. Meyer’s knowledge of Schultz and Matsuzaki
subfiles.from: J. J. Osten, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation field offices
subfiles.about: Reports Meyer’s account of Japanese efforts to find alternative oil and gasoline supplies.
subfiles.summary: Clarence E. Meyer described Schultz and Matsuzaki as acquaintances from the Japanese oil industry. He said a Tokyo newspaper reported that Matsuzaki was traveling to the United States to establish Mexican oil connections for the Japanese government because Japan feared losing supplies from the United States and the Dutch East Indies. Meyer agreed to seek further information through his New York contacts.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Taiyo Sekiyu Kaisha gasoline negotiations
subfiles.from: M. B. Rhodes, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation headquarters and field divisions
subfiles.about: Reviews extensive inquiries into Schultz, Matsuzaki and proposed purchases of high-octane gasoline for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report consolidates FBI leads from several field offices concerning a proposed purchase of 7,500 to 20,000 drums of aviation gasoline per month, backed by a $500,000 letter of credit. It traces negotiations involving Matsuzaki, Schultz, Neblett, Blodgett and Logan and discusses contacts with Gulf, Union, General Petroleum, Seaboard and other oil companies. Investigators found no clear violation of the Neutrality or Registration Acts but recommended continuing the inquiry for national-defense purposes.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of FBI letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of an FBI letter dated July 13, 1940.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State formally acknowledges and thanks the FBI for its July 13 letter. The page contains no substantive discussion of the investigation.

subfiles.title: Senator Barkley’s inquiry about scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s protest against exporting 300,000 tons of scrap iron and steel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Barkley sends Secretary Hull a telegram from J. C. Miller of the American Rolling Mill Company. He requests information that he can transmit to Miller about the proposed export and its effect on domestic scrap supplies.

subfiles.title: J. C. Miller telegram protesting scrap exports
subfiles.about: Protests the sale and export of 300,000 tons of scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miller argues that scrap shortages already force large consumers to pay premiums. He warns that the proposed shipment would worsen shortages and hamper the steel industry’s cooperation in the national emergency.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Barkley
subfiles.about: Explains the new licensing controls on exports of iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the presidential proclamations and regulations of July 2 and July 26, 1940. He states that the new export-control system permits the government to curtail or prohibit scrap exports whenever national defense requires it and returns Miller’s telegram.

subfiles.title: Senator Bone’s transmittal of Bellingham Iron Works protest
subfiles.about: Forwards T. W. Reid’s protest against exporting scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bone submits a telegram from the president of Bellingham Iron Works for the Department’s information. The telegram concerns the proposed export of 300,000 tons of scrap iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: T. W. Reid telegram protesting scrap exports
subfiles.about: Calls for withholding a 300,000-ton scrap shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reid warns that the shipment would harm American iron and steel industries. He also argues that it would jeopardize the national-defense program and asks Bone to act.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Bone
subfiles.about: Describes presidential export controls applicable to scrap iron and steel.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the July 2 and July 26 proclamations and regulations. He explains that scrap exports can now be licensed, curtailed or prohibited in the interest of national defense and returns Reid’s telegram.

subfiles.title: Transfer sheet for file 894.24/1008
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of document 894.24/1008 to another decimal-file location.
subfiles.summary: The single-page sheet directs that the item formerly numbered 894.24/1008 be filed under 811.20(D) Regulations/405. It contains no substantive account of the transferred document.

subfiles.title: Representative Johnson’s request for investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent communication concerning scrap exports and requests information for a reply.
subfiles.summary: Johnson asks the State Department to investigate the enclosed statements and send him the information needed to answer his constituent. He also requests return of the enclosure and asks for favorable consideration.

subfiles.title: Ralph Goeth telegram protesting scrap exports
subfiles.about: Protests the proposed export of 300,000 tons of scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Goeth states that an apparent scrap shortage already exists. He argues that the sale would burden iron and steel producers during a national emergency.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Representative Johnson
subfiles.about: Explains the new scrap-export licensing system and returns Goeth’s telegram.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the presidential proclamations and regulations of July 2 and July 26. He says the export-control system enables the government to curtail or prohibit scrap exports when national defense requires and returns the constituent telegram.

subfiles.title: Preparation of 500 flasks of quicksilver for shipment to Japan
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports financing and anticipated routing of a Mexican quicksilver shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi-Shoji-Kaisha of San Francisco established a $90,750 credit in Mexico City to buy 500 flasks of quicksilver at $181.50 each. The material was to pass in bond through San Francisco en route to Japan, probably after shipment from Manzanillo. No shipment date was available.

subfiles.title: Senator Overton’s acknowledgment concerning war-material exports
subfiles.about: Thanks Welles for information about war-material shipments to Japan, especially scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Overton acknowledges Welles’s July 31 letter. He expresses thanks for the information on shipments of war material and scrap iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: Tin smelters in Japan and wolfram shipments through Manchuria
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits consular reports on Japanese tin smelting and tungsten shipments through Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards confidential letters from the American consuls at Osaka and Dairen. The Dairen information indicates that Chinese tungsten ore had moved to Germany through Manchuria and the Trans-Siberian Railway. The Osaka report identifies Japanese tin smelters and states that Mitsubishi’s Osaka works produced 94 percent of Japan’s refined tin in 1936.

subfiles.title: List of tin smelters and refineries in Japan
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, American Consulate, Osaka
subfiles.about: Provides a purportedly complete list of Japanese tin smelters and refineries.
subfiles.summary: Allison reports that Mitsubishi’s Osaka Smelting Works dominates Japanese tin production and allegedly produced 94 percent of the national total in 1936. Most other listed facilities recovered tin from scrap sheet metal, cans and similar material rather than raw ore. The enclosure supplies names and addresses for plants in Tokyo, Osaka, Yokohama, Kobe, Hiroshima Prefecture and Hokkaido.

subfiles.title: Chinese tungsten shipments to Germany through Manchuria
subfiles.from: A. S. Chase, American Consulate, Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports recent movement of Chinese tungsten ore to Germany via Manchuria and Siberia.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source told Chase that Chinese tungsten ore had recently traveled to Germany through Manchuria and the Trans-Siberian Railway. The volume was unknown, and Chase inferred that the shipments came through North China rather than directly from South China to Dairen.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Universal Oil Products and Japan Gasoline Company contracts
subfiles.about: Records Saneyoshi’s presentation concerning two petroleum-technology contracts with Universal Oil Products.
subfiles.summary: Morishima and Saneyoshi discussed Universal’s refusal to provide data under contracts made in 1928 and 1938. Saneyoshi distinguished ordinary cracking-plant information from high-octane aviation-gasoline technology and described financial losses caused by Universal’s nonperformance. Hamilton noted the presentation but said the Department could add nothing to Berle’s recent statement to the Japanese ambassador.

subfiles.title: Berle’s conversation with Ambassador Horinouchi
subfiles.about: Discusses possible performance of the 1928 cracking-plant contract in exchange for withdrawal of related litigation.
subfiles.summary: Berle told Horinouchi that the ordinary cracking-plant contract appeared outside the moral embargo, unlike the high-octane contract. Horinouchi indicated that the Japan Gasoline Company would probably withdraw its action if deliveries resumed. A note records that Colonel Maxwell and the Defense Commission saw no national-defense reason to block the contract.

subfiles.title: Halle inquiry about the 1928 Japan Gasoline Company contract
subfiles.about: Records H. J. Halle’s telephone inquiry about whether Universal could fulfill its 1928 contract.
subfiles.summary: Halle reported that Saneyoshi had said the Department would not object to performance of the cracking-plant contract. Moseley replied that he knew Berle had met the ambassador but did not know the conversation’s substance. Halle emphasized his desire to cooperate with the government while arguing that the information was available elsewhere and would not injure American interests.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Enterprise Foundry correspondence
subfiles.about: Refers an enclosed communication for consideration and requests a report.
subfiles.summary: The Senate referral asks the Department to give the enclosed communication appropriate consideration. It requests a report to accompany return of the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Enterprise Foundry protest against scrap exports
subfiles.about: Requests Senator Mead’s help in stopping exports of approximately 300,000 tons of scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Verian asserts that a domestic scrap shortage already exists. He argues that the export would burden American iron and steel producers during the national emergency and asks that U.S. resources be preserved.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Mead
subfiles.about: Explains licensing controls on iron and steel scrap exports and returns Verian’s letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the July 2 and July 26 export-control proclamations and regulations. He states that the government can curtail or prohibit scrap exports when necessary for national defense. Verian’s letter is returned with the reply.

subfiles.title: Greene letter enclosing article on the 1918 embargo
subfiles.about: Submits an Amerasia article as a precedent for economic sanctions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene encloses Henry H. Douglas’s article about a successful American embargo against Japan in 1918. He argues that the episode provides a useful and generally overlooked precedent for effective economic sanctions.

subfiles.title: A Bit of American History—Successful Embargo Against Japan in 1918
subfiles.about: Argues that American economic pressure in 1918 forced Japan to reduce its military intervention in Siberia.
subfiles.summary: Douglas recounts Japan’s dispatch of roughly 72,500 troops to Siberia despite an agreement for a much smaller intervention force. He says the United States suspended licenses for cotton exports to Japan and silk imports after diplomatic protests failed, prompting the withdrawal of more than 50,000 Japanese troops by the end of 1918. The article presents this episode as evidence that a modern embargo could restrain Japan because of its dependence on American strategic supplies.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene’s letter and enclosed article on economic sanctions.
subfiles.summary: Yost confirms receipt of Greene’s August 14 letter and the magazine reprint. He states that the communication will receive careful attention in the Department.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on aviation gasoline stocks at Hainan
subfiles.about: Points to a Grew telegram concerning Japanese accumulation of aviation gasoline in South China and Hainan.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes reports that Japanese buyers placed orders with major American oil companies for gasoline in drums. Delivery was reportedly intended for South China and Hainan before October 1, 1940. The original record is cross-referenced to another file.

subfiles.title: Morishima’s thanks concerning the Universal Oil case
subfiles.about: Records Morishima’s thanks for developments following Berle’s conversation with the Japanese ambassador.
subfiles.summary: Morishima reviewed the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline Company dispute without adding new facts. He said Berle had told the ambassador that the Department expected to contact Halle within a few days about the changed position.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a committee letter urging broader controls on exports of war-useful material to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note cites page six of the August 1940 issue of The Sign and an enclosure submitted by Roger S. Greene’s committee. It records a proposal that export controls be expanded to all material and equipment useful for war.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products letter enclosing litigation agreement
subfiles.from: H. J. Halle, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Submits an agreement separating the 1928 contract claim from the Japan Gasoline Company litigation.
subfiles.summary: Halle explains that the parties’ lawyers signed an agreement removing claims for breach of the 1928 contract while Universal remained able to perform it. He states that both Universal and Saneyoshi approved the arrangement and asks whether it is satisfactory to the Department.

subfiles.title: Stipulation in Japan Gasoline Co. v. Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.from: Attorneys for Japan Gasoline Company and Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.to: United States District Court for the District of Delaware
subfiles.about: Provides for amendment of the complaint if Universal supplies specified cracking-process information under the 1928 contract.
subfiles.summary: Universal agrees to furnish process-flow diagrams, construction designs, specifications and technical advice for non-catalytic cracking and treating units. In exchange, Japan Gasoline Company will remove claims for specific performance or damages under the July 19, 1928 agreement. The stipulation identifies Hisashi Sekiguchi as the original Japanese contracting party.

subfiles.title: State Department approval of Universal–Japan Gasoline agreement
subfiles.about: States that the Department has no objection to the agreement resolving the 1928-contract issue.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges receipt of Universal’s letter and the attorneys’ agreement concerning the Japan Gasoline Company suit. He notes that the arrangement removes claims arising from the 1928 contract while Universal can comply with it. The Department offers no objection.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24
subfiles.about: Records charges or temporary routing of materials from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: The form lists several file references, dates and clerk notations. Much of the handwritten or typed routing information is indistinct, and it contains no substantive policy discussion.

subfiles.title: Assessment of “Japan’s Dependence on American Scrap”
subfiles.about: Endorses a Chinese Council for Economic Research memorandum on Japan’s dependence on American scrap.
subfiles.summary: The writer judges the June 1940 study to be well done. Particular praise is given to the summary on pages 13 through 15, which the writer believes is difficult to improve upon.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s Dependence on American Scrap
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s reliance on American iron and steel scrap and the likely effects of an embargo.
subfiles.summary: The study reports that Japan bought more than two million tons of American scrap in 1939 and that the United States supplied 89 percent of Japanese scrap imports. It reviews foreign sources, wartime export restrictions and the Japanese steel industry’s heavy use of scrap in open-hearth furnaces. The memorandum argues that other markets could not replace American supplies and begins assessing pig iron and ore as alternatives; the document continues beyond page 358.
